cards.title: Five core finance practices to run an ecommerce brand
cards.summary: A closing checklist of five financial operating habits—margin literacy, live dashboards, new/returning separation, cash vs P&L plays, and constraint diagnosis.
cards.use_when: Setting your store's monthly financial operating rhythm or auditing which finance disciplines your team is missing before scaling spend.
steps: 1) Know your gross margin and calculate it correctly: identify variable costs, and distinguish product margin from gross margin and how each flows into contribution margin. Use these definitions consistently across the team.

2) Define your metrics and build live dashboards—not daily ROAS reports. Track acquisition MER, profit contribution, and ideally LTGP to CAC. The source argues weekly ROAS reporting is unproductive for core decision-making.

3) Separate new vs returning customer metrics: track new-customer economics, acquisition MER, new-customer profit contribution, new-customer revenue and new-customer cohort size separately, because the underlying levers differ (and feed forecasting).

4) Know the difference between a cash play and a P&L play: if your limiter is the cash conversion cycle, pushing budgets up can raise interest expense and compress MER with no benefit. Keep marketing and inventory teams communicating on SKU inventory position so you can trade profit/MER efficiency to turn inventory into cash.

5) Use the P&L to identify the constraint in the business: structure it out, set KPIs at each level, and when you fall below target look above that level in the P&L to find what changed and which lever to pull.
Attribute the daily-vs-weekly ROAS stance to the source as an opinion, not a universal rule.
caveats: The daily-vs-weekly ROAS preference is the presenter's opinion, not an established benchmark.
The five-point list is a summary framework; it does not define numeric thresholds for any metric.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Structure your P&L as a constraint-diagnosis tool
cards.summary: Read the P&L line by line, set KPIs at each level, and when a KPI drops look one level up to find the changed lever and correct course.
cards.use_when: When a store's profit or efficiency metric falls below target and you need to locate the actual constraint rather than reflexively cutting ad spend.
steps: 1) Structure your P&L so each level has a clear definition (revenue, product margin, gross margin, contribution margin, profitability).
2) Set a target KPI for each level.
3) When you start falling below KPI at a given level, look above that level in the P&L to understand what changed—which variable cost, margin, or efficiency levers moved.
4) Pull the specific lever that rectifies the deviation and course-correct back to target rather than adjusting budgets arbitrarily.
5) Per the source, this is the single overarching purpose of the P&L: to identify the constraint in the business. Treat the P&L as a diagnostic map, not a reporting artifact.

The source's example: if it's not marketing spend or marketing efficiency, the real limiter may be the cash conversion cycle, in which case pushing budget up only adds interest expense and compresses MER.
caveats: The source does not specify exact KPI targets or tolerances; you must set them for your own business.
The practice assumes a correctly structured P&L where each level's variable costs are properly assigned.

cards.title: Budget brand as a P&L expense line, not just performance marketing
cards.summary: High-quality brand associations, messaging and creative can drive purchases that performance ads would not, so brand deserves deliberate budget allocation.
cards.use_when: Deciding store budget allocation between performance marketing and brand-building (creative campaigns, positioning work) as you scale.
steps: 1) Recognize that some purchases are driven by perception of quality created through overarching associations, messaging, and campaign creative—the source describes two personal purchases that happened through brand, not through a performance ad or Google ad.
2) Do not understate brand's role: the source says it becomes unbelievably important as you continue to scale.
3) Treat brand as a budget allocation—an expense on the P&L—rather than an optional residual of leftover ad budget.
4) Apply to ecommerce: invest in the campaign shoots and creative that shape quality perception on PDPs and in ads, and account for that spend when calculating contribution margin.
Note this is the presenter's judgment from anecdote, not measured attribution.
caveats: The two purchases cited are personal anecdotes; they are examples, not proof of a generalizable result.
Brand's effect may be hard to attribute in standard performance reporting—avoid forcing brand spend into a last-click metric.
cards.source_name: Everything You Need to Know About Finance in eCommerce.docx

cards.title: Align marketing strategy with SKU inventory to prioritize cash turnover
cards.summary: When cash is the constraint, deliberately accept lower profitability or MER to move inventory into cash, coordinating marketing and inventory teams.
cards.use_when: Replenishment, pricing or promotion planning when a store is cash-constrained and holding slow-moving SKUs.
steps: 1) Maintain constant communication between the marketing team (or agency) and whoever owns inventory, covering inventory position across the different SKUs.

2) Sequence a cash play before a P&L play when the cash conversion cycle is the limiter rather than marketing efficiency: the source says there's no point raising budgets arbitrarily if it just increases interest expenses and compresses MER.
3) Where inventory is overstocked, apply strategies that intentionally decrease profitability, decrease acquisition MER or decrease efficiency in order to prioritize turnover of inventory into cash.
4) Evaluate whether that trade makes the business overall healthier before executing.
This is an inventory-merchandising decision, not a universal rule to discount.
caveats: The source frames this as situational—only when cash conversion cycle is the actual constraint.
It gives no specific discount depth, turnover target or interest threshold; decide those from your own numbers.
